messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 76

Amin is twenty-five years old, a journalist for a local news outlet in a sprawling West African city. He has been seeing me for six weeks, referred by a colleague who noticed he could no longer sit through an editorial meeting without his hands shaking. He comes to session straight from work, still smelling of petrol and dust, his phone face down on the arm of the chair.

He tells the story the way he would file a report: clean, chronological, with the details in the right order. But his voice drops near the end of every sentence, as if the last words fall into a hole.

Eighteen months ago, Amin was assigned to cover a protest at a government building. He had done this dozens of times before—stand at the edge of the crowd, notebook out, camera hanging from his neck. That afternoon, the police arrived in a wave of blue. He remembers the sound of a single tear-gas canister, then two, then the air turning white and sour. He ran with the crowd, but an officer grabbed his collar and threw him face-first onto the concrete. He remembers the weight of a boot on his back, the smell of his own blood mixing with the dust, the officer shouting something about “journalists who think they are special.”

He was held for four hours in a holding cell. They did not beat him again, but they left him on the floor, hands cuffed too tight, the metal cutting into his wrists. When they let him go, he walked home in the dark, his camera still around his neck, the lens cracked. He did not call his girlfriend, Didi. He did not tell his editor. He showered, ate a piece of bread, and went to sleep.

At first, he thought he had moved on. He filed a story about the protest, but he left out the part about being arrested. He told himself it was irrelevant. But within weeks, he noticed small changes: he began crossing the street to avoid a police station he had walked past every day for years. The sound of a motorbike backfiring made him drop to a crouch in the middle of the sidewalk. He stopped covering protests altogether, telling his editor he was “tired of the beat.”

Didi noticed first. She would touch his shoulder and he would flinch, his whole body going rigid before he could stop it. He stopped wanting to go out to markets or crowded restaurants. He told her he was just stressed, working too hard. But at night, he could not sleep. He would lie awake, replaying the sound of the officer’s boot, the pressure of the handcuffs, the way his own voice cracked when he asked for water and no one answered. Some nights he woke up already on his feet, fists clenched, breathing so fast he thought his chest would split.

Now, in session, he sits still, but his eyes move constantly—to the window, to the door, back to the window. He has a habit of checking his phone every few minutes, though he never seems to read the messages. He tells me his editor has put him on feature stories now, soft pieces about local artisans and school reopening. He hates it. He wants to do real reporting again, but every time he thinks about going back to a protest, his stomach turns and his throat tightens.

He is still with Didi, but the relationship is fraying. She has asked him to talk to her, to tell her what happened. He cannot. He says the words get stuck, like they are made of something too heavy to push out. He knows she is frustrated. He knows she is scared. But he cannot find a way to let her in.

The PCL-5 score of 76, taken two weeks ago, confirms what I see: his avoidance is almost total, his hypervigilance constant, his intrusive memories unwelcome visitors that arrive without warning. He does not want to be broken. He wants his work back. He wants to hold Didi without flinching. But right now, he is still in that holding cell, eighteen months later, and he does not know how to leave.
